Revealer
rē-vēl´ĕr
n. (one who uncovers what is hidden; a divine title confessed by Nebuchadnezzar)
From Latin revelare, to draw back the veil, from velum, a veil. Daniel 2:47 renders the Aramaic participle of gelah, to uncover, in Nebuchadnezzar's own confession — a pagan king's title for the God of Israel.

Biblical Definition

Nebuchadnezzar has demanded the impossible — the dream and its interpretation — and the wise men of Babylon have told him no man on earth can do it. When Daniel does, the king confesses more than he knows: “The king answered unto Daniel, and said, Of a truth it is, that your God is a God of gods, and a Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets, seeing thou couldest reveal this secret” (Daniel 2:47). Daniel had already refused the credit and set the title where it belonged: “But there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets, and maketh known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Thy dream, and the visions of thy head upon thy bed, are these” (Daniel 2:28). The ground of it is what God is in Himself: “He revealeth the deep and secret things: he knoweth what is in the darkness, and the light dwelleth with him” (Daniel 2:22). Darkness hides nothing from Him because the light is where He lives. And the settled pattern of His self-disclosure is through His appointed servants: “Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets” (Amos 3:7). Revelation is not something men extract. It is something God gives, and He gives it through a word.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a revealer as one who discloses or makes known; one who discovers to the view what was before hidden or unknown.

expand to see more

REVEALER, n. One that discloses or makes known; that which shows or makes known.

REVEAL, v.t. [L. revelo; re and velo, to veil.] To disclose; to discover; to show; to make known something before unknown or concealed.

REVEAL, v.t. To disclose, discover or make known from heaven. God has been pleased to reveal his will to man.

REVELATION, n. The act of disclosing or discovering to others what was before unknown to them. In theology, the disclosure or communication of truth to men by God himself, or by his authorized agents.

SECRET, n. Something studiously concealed; a thing kept from general knowledge.

Key Scripture

Daniel 2:47 — "The king answered unto Daniel, and said, Of a truth it is, that your God is a God of gods, and a Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets, seeing thou couldest reveal this secret."

Daniel 2:28 — "But there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets, and maketh known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Thy dream, and the visions of thy head upon thy bed, are these;"

Daniel 2:22 — "He revealeth the deep and secret things: he knoweth what is in the darkness, and the light dwelleth with him."

Amos 3:7 — "Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets."

Modern Corruption

Revelation is treated as an ongoing private supply — impressions, words, downloads — rather than as the closed and sufficient Scripture God has given.

expand to see more

Daniel 2 is the favourite chapter of every movement that claims fresh revelation, and it argues against them. Daniel receives the secret, and the secret is immediately public, verifiable, and about God's kingdom rather than Daniel's life — he does not get a private word for his own guidance. The New Apostolic Reformation, the prophetic conference circuit, and the personal-word culture that trickles down from them all invert this. Where the modern claim cannot be tested, Deuteronomy 18 has already given the test and the penalty for failing it.

The dictionary is cessationist with the Reformed mainstream, and the positive ground is the better argument. Hebrews opens by saying God spoke in time past by the prophets and has in these last days spoken by His Son, which is a completion and not a pause. The 1689 confesses that those former ways of revealing His will are now ceased, and that Scripture is therefore most necessary and sufficient. God is still the revealer of secrets, as Daniel 2:22 says He is by nature. What He has revealed, He has put in a book, and the sufficiency of that book is the comfort of the ordinary Christian who has no dream to report.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Aramaic gelah (H1541), to uncover, reveal; Hebrew galah (H1540), to uncover; sod (H5475), a secret counsel; Greek apokalupto (G601), to unveil.

expand to see more

Aramaic gelah (H1541) — to reveal, uncover; the participle behind revealer of secrets.

Aramaic raz (H7328) — a mystery, secret; the word for what the king demanded.

Hebrew sod (H5475) — intimate counsel; Amos 3:7, the secret told to His servants.

Hebrew nabi (H5030) — a prophet; the appointed channel, not the source.

Greek apokalupsis (G602) — an unveiling; the New Testament word for the same act.

Usage

"“A revealer of secrets” — confessed by a pagan king."

"“The light dwelleth with him” — darkness hides nothing from where He lives."

"“He revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets” — given through a word, not extracted."
